{"meta":{"search_id":"qK8qRwaFtEST81pLx40LKQ","total":45962,"offset":0,"limit":3,"sort_field":null,"sort_order":"ASC","sorted_by_relevance":true,"properties":{"URL":"https:/reporter.nih.gov/search/qK8qRwaFtEST81pLx40LKQ/projects"}},"results":[{"fiscal_year":2027,"project_num":"5R01AI187493-03","organization":{"org_name":"UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS HLTH SCI CTR HOUSTON","city":null,"country":null,"org_city":"HOUSTON","org_country":"UNITED STATES","org_state":"TX","org_state_name":null,"dept_type":"PUBLIC HEALTH & PREV MEDICINE","fips_country_code":null,"org_duns":["800771594"],"org_ueis":["ZUFBNVZ587D4"],"primary_duns":"800771594","primary_uei":"ZUFBNVZ587D4","org_fips":"US","org_ipf_code":"578417","org_zipcode":"770305400","external_org_id":578417},"award_amount":413852,"principal_investigators":[{"profile_id":15605316,"first_name":"Victor","middle_name":"","last_name":"Lopez del Amo","is_contact_pi":true,"full_name":"Victor  Lopez del Amo","title":"ASSISTANT PROFESSOR"}],"project_start_date":"2024-11-13T00:00:00","project_end_date":"2029-10-31T00:00:00","abstract_text":"PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Several viruses such as yellow fever, Zika, Chikungunya, and dengue affect millions of people, causing over
300,000 deaths every year. These viruses are vectored through Aedes mosquito bites, transmitting the
pathogens between people. The use of insecticides to kill mosquitoes or vaccines to protect people against the
viruses has helped reduce the incidence of these diseases. However, these pathologies still represent a
continuing public health and economic burden in disease-endemic countries.
The advent of CRISPR has offered tremendous potential to solve this public health issue by providing new
technologies such as the genetic sterile insect technique (pgSIT) and gene drive approaches. 1) pgSIT relies on
the generation of two transgenic lines: a Cas9 strain and a line containing a set of guide-RNAs (gRNAs) targeting
genes involved in male sterility and female lethality or infertility. Therefore, the combined genetic cross of the
Cas9 and gRNAs lines produces only sterile male progeny. 2) CRISPR gene drives allow for engineering wild
populations due to their ability to self-propagate and spread engineered traits. Gene-drive strategies to fight
malaria aim to either spread beneficial cassettes to confer pathogen resistance for population modification or to
propagate deleterious mutations for population suppression.
These strategies have demonstrated efficiency under laboratory conditions; however, there are important issues
that need addressing before these new technologies can be safely applied in the environment:
 1. pgSIT requires the maintenance and crossbreeding of two parental strains to obtain sterile males,
 involving time-consuming logistical efforts when scaling for field purposes.
 2. Cas9-based gene drives can introduce small insertions/deletions (indels) instead of replacing the wildtype
 allele with a copy of the gene drive element when the repair process fails. This represents one of the
 most significant obstacles to the field deployment of gene drives.
My proposed studies aim to tackle these concerns. First, I will design a Cas12 temperature-dependent system;
this strategy will only require one strain containing both Cas12a and gRNAs. It can be maintained at lower
temperatures like a regular strain but produces sterile males when switched to higher temperatures (Aim 1).
Additionally, I will address indel formation concerns by using the Cas12a nuclease that generates small deletions
still recognizable by the gene drive element to allows its full introgression (Aim 2).
Future technologies born from this project’s groundwork could reduce the economic burden of dengue (and other
viruses) disease and increase our readiness for an eventual worsening of the disease incidence.","project_title":"Advancing CRISPR-Based Genome Editing Strategies for managing Aedes aegypti mosquito populations","agency_code":"NIH","project_detail_url":"https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/11458941"},{"fiscal_year":2027,"project_num":"5R01AI175150-04","organization":{"org_name":"WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY","city":null,"country":null,"org_city":"SAINT LOUIS","org_country":"UNITED STATES","org_state":"MO","org_state_name":null,"dept_type":"MICROBIOLOGY/IMMUN/VIROLOGY","fips_country_code":null,"org_duns":["068552207"],"org_ueis":["L6NFUM28LQM5"],"primary_duns":"068552207","primary_uei":"L6NFUM28LQM5","org_fips":"US","org_ipf_code":"9083901","org_zipcode":"631304862","external_org_id":9083901},"award_amount":608852,"principal_investigators":[{"profile_id":6417435,"first_name":"L.","middle_name":"David","last_name":"Sibley","is_contact_pi":true,"full_name":"L. David Sibley","title":"PROFESSOR"}],"project_start_date":"2023-11-09T00:00:00","project_end_date":"2028-10-31T00:00:00","abstract_text":"PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Cryptosporidium is a wide-spread enteric pathogen that causes severe diarrheal disease in
immunocompromised patients and infants, especially in the developing world. There are more than 20
described species of Cryptosporidium some of which show narrow host ranges while others are quite broad. C.
parvum has a relatively broad host range infecting many agricultural animals and causing zoonotic infections in
humans. C. parvum is further divided into subtypes that undergo recombination in the wild often resulting in in
differences in host range, infectivity, and virulence. The factors that control host range of C. parvum as well as
their pathogenicity in different hosts are largely unknown, presenting a major gap in our understanding of this
important group of parasites. In preliminary studies, we have defined major virulence differences between
common laboratory variants of C. parvum during infection in immunocompromised mice. High-virulence
isolates are associated with elevated oocyst shedding and lethality, while low-virulence isolates cause only
mild, non-lethal infections. Whole genome sequencing identified numerous single nucleotide polymorphisms in
candidate genes that likely control these phenotypic differences. We recently developed a stem-cell derived
system for culturing differentiated intestinal enterocytes that allows complete development of C. parvum in
vitro, including production of viable oocysts. In preliminary studies, we tagged C. parvum isolates with
fluorescent reporters using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and used these lines to conduct genetic crosses in
vitro. Analysis of the recombinant progeny from crossed lines demonstrates that meiosis results in Mendelian
chromosome reassortment. In the proposed studies, we will cross fluorescently tagged virulent isolates with
avirulent isolates in vitro, sort recombinant progeny using FACS, and expand them in mice to select for genes
associated with increased fitness. The contributing loci will be mapped using Bulk Segregant Analysis to define
candidate genes that will be confirmed by CRISPR/Cas editing. These studies should lead to a molecular
understanding of pathogenicity of C. pavrum and may identify genes responsible for mediating infectivity and
host-range.","project_title":"Genetic Basis of Host Infectivity by Cryptosporidium","agency_code":"NIH","project_detail_url":"https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/11460320"},{"fiscal_year":2027,"project_num":"1I01RD001118-01","organization":{"org_name":"JAMES J PETERS VA  MEDICAL CENTER","city":null,"country":null,"org_city":"BRONX","org_country":"UNITED STATES","org_state":"NY","org_state_name":null,"dept_type":null,"fips_country_code":null,"org_duns":["040077133"],"org_ueis":["CZ6LSS7VPWY1"],"primary_duns":"040077133","primary_uei":"CZ6LSS7VPWY1","org_fips":"US","org_ipf_code":"481060","org_zipcode":"104683904","external_org_id":481060},"award_amount":null,"principal_investigators":[{"profile_id":1890709,"first_name":"STELLA","middle_name":"","last_name":"DRACHEVA","is_contact_pi":true,"full_name":"STELLA  DRACHEVA","title":"RESEARCH CAREER SCIENTIST"}],"project_start_date":"2026-10-01T00:00:00","project_end_date":"2030-09-30T00:00:00","abstract_text":"Significance to VA: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disorder of the central nervous
system (CNS), causing demyelination, neuronal injury, and progressive disability. In the U.S., approximately 1
million people live with MS, including 55,000–70,000 Veterans, with 18,000–20,000 receiving care through the
VHA annually. MS imposes a significant burden on Veterans, underscoring the urgent need for research to
elucidate its mechanisms and advance more effective treatments. Current therapies primarily target immune-
mediated damage but fail to promote remyelination. This project directly addresses that gap by focusing on
oligodendrocytes (OLIGs) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) to drive myelin repair.
Impact and Innovation: The proposed research aims to identify novel therapeutic targets for MS by focusing
on the epigenetic regulation of OPCs and OLIGs, which are critical for myelin repair. The results have the
potential to uncover new pathways involved in remyelination and to prioritize small molecules for further
therapeutic development. The project contains many innovations, including (1) our novel fluorescence-
activated nuclei sorting method (FANS) to isolate OPC and OLIG nuclei from human postmortem brain tissue,
enabling the first-ever epigenetic profiling of purified OPCs and OLIGs in MS, (2) leveraging paired
transcriptomic and epigenetic datasets and applying a state-of-the-art bioinformatics framework to construct
gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and identify transcription factors and chromatin regulators driving MS and
aging-related changes, and (3) integrating in silico systems pharmacology with in vitro models and CRISPR to
predict and test small-molecule candidates capable of reversing MS-specific and MS-and-aging overlapping
transcriptional changes.
Specific Aims: We will test the following hypotheses: (1) genes regulating myelin production in OLIGs and
proliferation/differentiation in OPCs are epigenetically silenced in MS lesions. (2) less pronounced, silencing of
these genes occurs in normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) from MS donors. (3) MS and aging share
significant epigenetic and transcriptional alterations in OPCs and OLIGs, with both distinct and overlapping
targets for remyelination therapies. (4) MS-associated transcriptional signatures (MS-specific or shared
between MS and aging), represent distinct yet complementary therapeutic targets for future MS treatments.
 To test these hypotheses, we will pursue three aims. (1) We will characterize the transcriptional and
epigenetic landscape of OPCs and OLIGs from MS donors and controls. This will define cell-type-specific
regulatory changes in MS lesions and NAWM. (2) We will identify differentially expressed genes and regulatory
elements associated with MS and aging and construct GRNs to uncover mechanisms contributing to age-
related remyelination failure. (3) we will use in silico drug prediction and validate candidate small molecules in
oligodendrocyte-like cells (ioOLIGs) to reverse MS-associated transcriptional and epigenetic signatures.
Methodology: We will perform FANS to isolate OPCs and OLIGs from postmortem brains, followed by RNA-
seq, ChIP-seq, and 10x multiome assays. Bioinformatic analysis will construct GRNs, identify key regulators,
and use SigCom LINCS software for in silico drug prediction. Selected drug candidates will be validated in
ioOLIG models through CRISPR-based perturbations.
Path to Translation/Implementation: Our integrative approach will uncover shared and distinct regulatory
pathways underlying MS and aging, laying the groundwork for novel therapies targeting remyelination failure.
In the short term, we will identify epigenetic markers of remyelination, link transcriptional changes to regulatory
elements, and prioritize small molecules for preclinical testing. Long term, our findings will provide a foundation
for developing MS therapies that promote remyelination and mitigate age-related decline, ultimately improving
outcomes for Veterans.","project_title":"Epigenetic Alterations in Human Oligodendroglia: Prioritizing Therapeutic Targets for Multiple Sclerosis","agency_code":"VA","project_detail_url":"https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/11299228"}]}
